title: How Eve Online Leverages Head Based Sampling to Observe "Fun"
gist: EVE Online's observability lead explains why a 20-year-old, single-logical-processor Python/C++ MMO uses 100% head-based sampling that blends deterministic and exponential-moving-average sampling, targeting 'at least one of everything' at roughly 50-60 million events per day in Honeycomb. The talk exposes tradeoffs for SLOs, costs and legacy migration.

themes.theme: Head-based sampling forced by legacy constraints

insights.claim: EVE Online uses 100% head-based sampling rather than tail-based because its stackless Python 2.7 runs on one logical processor and cannot emit spans fast enough for tail sampling without harming the simulation.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Legacy runtime limits dictate observability architecture; modernization cost is a hidden drag for old systems.
insights.locator: The first part is talking about head versus tail

insights.claim: Tail-based sampling requires sending all spans to one central place, which the speaker avoids because he dislikes going blind in large chunks of the ecosystem; without a relay, degradation shows up as specific parts failing to reach Honeycomb.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Centralized collectors are single points of observability failure.
insights.locator: My bias against that is that I don't like

insights.claim: The speaker concludes that tail-based sampling would occasionally be nice but the ROI of building the infrastructure and solving performance challenges is not high enough to justify it.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Challenges the default industry assumption that tail sampling is the superior approach.
insights.locator: Ultimately, to tie this all back together

insights.claim: Exponential moving average sampling keyed on protobuf message type URL samples less what it sees often and more what it sees rarely, automatically suppressing noise like 500 players switching ship skins or bullets in flight.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Adaptive sampling decouples telemetry cost from traffic bursts.
insights.locator: Then we get into the exponential moving average

insights.claim: With about 30,000 messages per second, a key space of ~2,000 message types and 35 ingress instances, a per-instance EMA goal of 1 in 3,000 cannot drop below roughly 60 million events a day, creating a high watermark that cost planning must respect.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Cost floor in EMA sampling scales with key space and instance count, not just traffic.
insights.locator: Then you have these three key components

insights.claim: Because EMA always samples something per key, the system guarantees at least one of every message type is seen, allowing the team to infer rates from sample rates and separate debugging signal from noise.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Rare-event visibility is preserved cheaply.
insights.locator: Another big part and purpose of why we smashed

insights.claim: The legacy simulation, a deterministic lockstep engine called Destiny, must be sampled deterministically because dynamic sampling would hurt performance, and Honeycomb's extrapolation from sample rates has proven within about plus or minus 300 units even for sparse data.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Extrapolation from sampled traces can be reliable enough for capacity decisions.
insights.locator: Our simulation engine is a deterministic lockstep

insights.claim: Growth in the EMA key space can cause odd behavior in distributed EMA; this is unlikely at human pace but the speaker flags that the rate at which AI could generate new message types might become a problem.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: AI-driven code proliferation may inflate telemetry key spaces and costs.
insights.quote: The AI rate, that might be a problem later.
insights.locator: When your key space grows

insights.claim: The team targets about 90% quota utilization, running around 50 million events a day, which leaves headroom to temporarily crank up sampling (the 'Eye of Sauron') via LaunchDarkly feature flags without overage bills; forgotten flags trigger automated spend alerts.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Pre-provisioned quota headroom plus flag-based escalation is a practical observability FinOps pattern.
insights.locator: Another technique we have is targeting 90%

insights.claim: Merging request and response into a single span by splitting the attribute namespace cut tracing cost by half, and not tracing best-effort client notices removed a large amount of quota.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Instrumentation design choices can deliver bigger savings than sampling rates.
insights.locator: Another trick that we did was we integrated

insights.claim: Stable player counts (spikes from roughly 30K to 40K around expansions) mean the high watermark is predictable, which makes observability spend plannable; the approach fits products with low burstiness.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Observability cost models depend on workload variance, so bursty products need different designs.
insights.locator: The high watermark is very important

insights.claim: Worker coroutines such as the five-minute bounty payout are broken out so traces never start as a root there, preventing giant traces and allowing separate sampling.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Tracing legacy batch patterns requires targeted exceptions.
insights.locator: One of the things that we first learned

insights.claim: Head-based sampling preserves true success/failure ratios, helping SLO fidelity, but SLOs on rare deterministically sampled events (such as 1 in 1,000 UI interactions) are dangerous because one error can burn the whole error budget.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Naive SLOs on sparse data produce false alarms.
insights.locator: There's another interesting side effect of this technique

insights.claim: Emitting spans from desktop clients forces 1-in-1,000 sampling decisions early in a trace, hiding important rare actions like anchoring a space station; the team plans to stop client span instrumentation and decide sampling in a trusted network, using averaged metrics for latency.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Client-side tracing at scale is costly and low-signal compared to server-side sampling.
insights.locator: We talked a little bit about the actual desktop client

insights.claim: Emitting spans per client frame across 30,000 GPUs has broken things, illustrating the cost of over-instrumenting real-time clients.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Instrumentation overhead can itself cause incidents.

themes.theme: EVE Online scale and legacy modernization

insights.claim: EVE Online is a single-sharded MMO with about 1.7 million lines of C/C++, 3.4 million lines of stackless Python 2.7, 2.6 million lines of SQL and 53 million lines of YAML, with a migration under way to Quasar (Kubernetes, Go, gRPC, protobuf, RabbitMQ, NATs).
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Illustrates the size of technical debt in long-lived live-service games and the cost of modernization.
insights.locator: 20 Years of EVE Development

insights.claim: The legacy and Quasar systems together process about 30,000 messages per second (estimated at about 60,000 in the Q&A), with a production database of roughly 17-18 TB, and the market sees about half a million transactions per day moving 12 billion items.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Provides scale benchmarks for real-time shared-state simulation workloads.
insights.locator: What is EVE Online?

insights.claim: Titan ships in EVE are worth roughly 1,000 euros each in real-currency terms, and the biggest battle cost roughly $387,000 with about 257 of them, which is why distinguishing high-value events from cosmetic ones drives what gets traced.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Real-money stakes in virtual economies make data integrity and observability a business matter.
insights.locator: The In-Game Experience

insights.claim: A test with 500 players rapidly switching ship skins with rate limiters off generated as many messages as the whole universe (about 50,000 per second), and the new ship-skin system forced Quasar to be aware of every ship at every simulation tick, overloading the data engineering team.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Cosmetic features can create outsized infrastructure load in real-time systems.

insights.claim: Introducing tracing with a smart bomb test on 500 ships produced a trace with 35,000 spans and revealed unknown behaviors in the legacy system, which convinced the organization of observability's value.
insights.speaker: Nicholas Herring
insights.so_what: Observability can pay for itself by exposing hidden legacy behavior.
insights.locator: That became so real when we did an initial test
